paragraphs.text: Lesson 23, likes, dislikes, and preferences.
Conversation number one, expressing likes and dislikes.
Denise and Robert are business partners.
They're evaluating a new design for a website for their online store.
Let's listen to their conversation.
The designer sent us three possibilities for the site.
Here's the first one.
I think it looks good.
Hmm, I like the colors, but I'm not crazy about the format.
It seems kind of disorganized.
Actually, I didn't like it at first either, but then it grew on me.
The design is a bit unusual, but once you start exploring the website,
it's easy to get the hang of it.
Let me see the next one.
I love the way this design highlights the photos of our products.
They're really eye-catching, but I don't care for the font he used.
It's too small and hard to read.
This one has potential.
We can just ask him to increase the size of the text, but I don't like the logo at all.
Okay, well, here's number three.
I'm not a big fan of this look.
I think it's too formal.
What do you think of it?
Well, don't roll it out yet.
The design is pretty sophisticated.
I'd rather have a professional-looking website than one that looks amateurish.
I can't stand the animated logo on the top though.
It's distracting.
Could he ask the designer to take it out?
Well, I don't mind the animation, but if it bothers you, I guess I'll ask him to make some
changes and then send us new designs.
But I hate to delay the project any further.
Conversation, Vocabulary, and Phrases.
In this dialogue, we hear a number of phrases for expressing likes, dislikes, and preferences.
You learned a few of these expressions in the lesson about hobbies, but not every expression
can be used in every case.
First, let's learn phrases for liking something.
I like.
I like Italian food.
I like rock music.
I like learning languages.
To express an even stronger feeling, you could say, I like it a lot.
Or I really like.
For example, I like this restaurant a lot.
I like my teacher a lot.
I really like my new apartment.
I really like playing tennis.
I really like my boyfriend's parents.
Another strong way to express your feelings is, I love.
For example, I love your haircut.
I love to read.
I love the way he writes.
And if you want to give even more emphasis, then use the phrase, I absolutely love.
For example, I absolutely love this dress.
I absolutely love traveling with my family.
These are the most common expressions.
I like is the weakest, and I absolutely love is the strongest.
You can use like and love for both nouns, like food, houses or apartments, music, movies,
movies, books, etc. and verbs, reading, learning, playing tennis, etc.
As mentioned in a previous lesson, after like and love, you can use either the two form or
the ing form of the verb with no difference in meaning.
I like to read is the same as I like reading.
By the way, be careful not to make the common mistake of saying, I like very much this city.
The correct way to say it is, I like this city very much.
Here are a few phrases for liking things that are used in more specific situations.
I'm fond of.
This phrase is used when you have a special, warm, emotional attachment to something.
For example, you could say, I'm fond of this photo.
It was taken on our honeymoon.
The expression I'm fond of can also be used for people who you have a special affection for.
Another way to express that you really like something is to say, I'm crazy about, or I'm
really into.
For example, I'm crazy about tennis, or I'm really into tennis.
One idiom for liking things is to say, it's right up my alley.
This expression means that some activity is perfect for a person's personality and interest.
For example, if Denise enjoys marketing and design, then the new website project is right
up her alley.
Finally, here's an interesting phrase that was used in the conversation.
I didn't like it at first, but then it grew on me.
It grew on me means you didn't like something initially, but then you began to like it as time
passed.
Now let's learn some phrases for disliking something.
We don't usually say, I dislike in English.
It's more typical to say, I don't like.
However, depending on the situation, you might want to express your dislike more indirectly.
These phrases are diplomatic and polite ways to say you don't like something.
I'm not a big fan of.
For example, I'm not a big fan of horror movies.
I'm not crazy about.
For example, I'm not crazy about this painting.
I don't care for.
For example, I don't care for spicy food.
I don't really like.
For example, I don't really like going to parties where I don't know anybody.
I don't really like my sister-in-law.
I don't really like video games.
It's not my thing, or it's not my cup of tea.
For example, skiing is not my thing.
Going to nightclubs is not my cup of tea.
These expressions are used only for activities, not for people or objects.
The first three phrases I'm not a big fan of.
I'm not crazy about, and I don't care for, are most typically used with objects.
The last phrases are used for activities, and the phrase I don't really like can be used
for people, objects, or activities.
If you want to express strong dislike, then you can use these phrases.
I can't stand.
For example, I can't stand Margaret.
She talks too much.
I can't stand it when people call me and don't leave a message.
I don't like it at all.
For example, I don't like this hotel at all.
I don't like Peter at all.
He seems dishonest.
I hate.
I hate tomatoes.
I hate going out in the rain.
I hate it when my kids fight with each other.
The expression I can't stand is used more for annoying things.
I don't like it at all is a strong statement of dislike, and I hate is the strongest statement.
A few other words for hate are loathe, detest, and despise, although these are less common.
One very common structure is to say, I hate it when, or I can't stand it when, and then
describe the situation that angers or annoys you.
In the conversation, we also heard a less strong way to use the word hate.
Denise said, I hate to delay the project any further.
This way of using the word hate means something more like I don't want to.
I don't want to delay the project any further, or I think it's unfortunate to delay the project
any further.
Conversation number two, expressing preferences.
After weeks of work, Denise and Robert have two designs, and need to make the final decision
between them.
Okay, here are the final designs.
Let's call them A and B.
Which one do you prefer?
They're really quite different.
Design A is very colorful and fun, and Design B has a more formal look.
I like the logo on A better, but I prefer the layout of B.
Robert, we need to just make a choice.
I'd really rather not ask for any more changes.
I think the designer is getting fed up.
Hold on now.
I'd rather take our time and not rush the decision.
What do you think?
I strongly prefer A. It's still professional looking, but it has more personality.
Plus, I like the way the menu is set up, and I think it's easier to navigate.
See, that's where we differ.
I tend to favor a more traditional format, whereas you'd like to experiment and be creative.
Actually, I asked a bunch of our employees, too, and they all prefer Design A.
Oh, well, I guess I'm outnumbered.
Alright, then.
Let's go with A.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
In this dialogue, we hear a few different phrases used to express preference.
They are the same in meaning, but there are a few details that are different.
After the expressions, I prefer, and I'd prefer, you can use a noun or a verb.
For example, I prefer the blue shirt.
It's nicer than the red one.
I prefer running to swimming.
I prefer to wake up early.
I'd prefer to check with the boss before making this decision.
We use I prefer for a general preference, and I'd prefer for a preference in a specific
situation.
After the expression, I'd rather, then you can only use a verb without, too.
For example, I'd rather watch TV than do my homework.
I'd rather live in a house than in an apartment.
I'd rather not go to the party.
I'm not feeling well.
I'd rather not spend more than a thousand dollars on a new computer.
The expression, I tend to favor, is used for general preferences, preferences that you usually
have all the time, not just in one specific situation.
For example, I tend to favor tea over coffee.
I tend to favor sci-fi movies over fantasy.
There are a lot of great dishes at this restaurant, but I tend to favor the seafood.
A simple and informal way to express your preference is, I like better or more.
For example, I like the first design better than the second one.
I like rock music more than country music.
I like reading poetry a lot better or a lot more than reading novels.
I like broccoli a little better or a little more than cauliflower.
Finally, what do you say if you have no preference?
Here are a few options.
Which one do you prefer?
Or which one do you like better?
If you have no preference, then say, it doesn't matter to me.
It makes no difference to me.
It's all the same to me.
I don't care.
Or I couldn't care less.
Be careful.
Those phrases, especially I couldn't care less, are a little bit rude.
If you don't have a preference and you want the other person to make the decision, then
you can say, it's up to you.
It's your decision.
It's your call.
You finished lesson 23.
Today's speaking task is to leave a message telling me about music, food, and activities
that you like and dislike.
Try to use the phrases from this lesson in your answer.
